paragraphs: Integrated Gradients assigns importance to input features to help explain a neural network’s prediction. This paper examines the mathematical foundations of that explanation method, particularly claims that its desirable axioms uniquely determine it. The authors identify differences between the function spaces used for Integrated Gradients and those in supporting mathematical work, which complicate earlier uniqueness arguments.

They show that adding an axiom called non-decreasing positivity establishes the uniqueness claims. They also investigate whether small input changes produce proportionally small attribution changes, a property called Lipschitz continuity. Their analysis identifies function classes where this property holds and others where it does not, making sensitivity a question about the functions involved rather than an unconditional property of the method.

The paper further connects axioms for a single reference input to analogous properties for distributions of reference inputs. Finally, it introduces an efficient way to identify internal neurons contributing to selected regions of an attribution map, with experiments validating that method. Together, these contributions clarify both the guarantees behind Integrated Gradients and how its explanations can be traced inside a network.
icml-2022-a-rigorous-study-of-integrated.tldr: The paper strengthens the mathematical foundations of Integrated Gradients and introduces an efficient method for tracing attribution regions to internal neurons.

paragraphs: Spectral clustering groups graph vertices by first representing them as points and then applying k-means. In the classical setup studied here, finding k clusters involves constructing coordinates from k eigenvectors of a matrix associated with the graph. The paper reexamines both the conditions under which this procedure works and the number of eigenvectors it needs.

Its first contribution is a tighter performance analysis that supports spectral clustering under a substantially weaker condition than earlier analyses considered. This expands the theoretical explanation of when the classical algorithm succeeds. Its second contribution shows that using fewer than k eigenvectors can produce better clustering for many practical instances, even though the desired number of clusters remains k.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the practical relevance of using fewer eigenvectors: the resulting clusterings are comparable to or better than those from the conventional choice. The findings therefore distinguish the number of groups being sought from the dimension of the representation used to find them. They support a smaller embedding in many instances, without asserting that it is always the better choice.
icml-2022-a-tighter-analysis-of-spectral.tldr: A tighter analysis supports spectral clustering under weaker conditions and shows that fewer eigenvectors can yield better clustering in many practical instances.

paragraphs: Federated learning becomes complicated when participating clients use neural networks with different architectures. Even networks with similar structures present difficulties because neuron order can vary and layers perform nonlinear transformations. FedHeNN addresses this setting by allowing each client to train a personalized network without requiring all participants to adopt a common architecture.

The framework uses representations of individual examples produced by peer clients to guide training on each client. This creates a way for models to benefit from one another’s learning despite architectural differences. A client can therefore choose a model suited to its local data and computing constraints while still receiving guidance from peers, including potentially more powerful models.

The reported experiments show better-performing client models in settings where architectures are either shared or different across participants. The contribution is consequently broader than accommodating heterogeneous networks alone: the same representation-based guidance also helps in the homogeneous setting evaluated. The central idea is to organize collaboration around what networks represent for examples, allowing architectural choices to remain local to each participant.
icml-2022-architecture-agnostic-federate.tldr: FedHeNN guides client training with peer representations, enabling federated collaboration among personalized networks with different architectures.

paragraphs: Bayesian additive regression trees estimate flexible relationships by combining many decision trees. Most existing versions divide feature space using one variable at a time, producing rectangular regions. This geometry can be poorly suited to structured inputs such as spatial locations, where valid regions may have irregular boundaries or lie on a manifold.

BAMDT combines two kinds of splits within each tree. Ordinary single-variable splits handle features without a known multivariate structure, including potentially high-dimensional inputs. New multivariate splits handle features whose joint geometry matters. These splits use stochastic spanning-tree bipartitions built on reference points, allowing flexible nonlinear boundaries while supporting efficient dimension-reduction computations.

This combination matters because one regression problem can contain both structured and unstructured features. The model can account for their different properties within the same ensemble instead of forcing every feature through rectangular partitions. Experiments with simulated data and Sacramento housing prices report superior performance for the proposed method. Those findings support the value of making tree boundaries responsive to the geometry of the structured inputs in the evaluated problems.
icml-2022-bamdt-bayesian-additive-semi-m.tldr: BAMDT combines ordinary and geometry-aware tree splits to model regression problems containing both unstructured and jointly structured features.

paragraphs: Few-shot image classification asks a model to adapt to new classification tasks using very little task-specific information. A central difficulty is that the new tasks can differ from those encountered during training. This paper studies that shift through the channels of learned image representations, asking whether the importance assigned to those channels transfers appropriately.

The authors show that a simple transformation applied channel by channel can substantially improve representation generalization on novel tasks at test time. The transformation is agnostic to the choice of dataset and training algorithm. Its significance is that a relatively simple change to existing features can expose a consequential weakness in how those features transfer between tasks.

Their analysis identifies severe channel bias: different tasks may require different channels to matter, while convolutional networks can fail to respond to that change or respond incorrectly. The findings connect transfer difficulty to the handling of channel importance, rather than treating a learned representation as equally suitable for every new task. They also motivate closer attention to this issue in the generalization of vision systems.
icml-2022-channel-importance-matters-in-.tldr: A simple channel-wise transformation improves few-shot transfer and reveals that learned channel importance can be poorly matched to new tasks.

paragraphs: Decision-focused learning trains a predictive model according to the quality of the decisions its predictions support. In the setting studied here, predicted values become cost coefficients in a discrete optimization problem. The paper reframes this process as learning to rank feasible solutions: the learned objective should place the better decisions ahead of worse ones.

This viewpoint does not depend on a particular optimization method or objective-function form. Building on it, the authors develop pointwise, pairwise, and listwise ranking losses. Given a subset of feasible solutions, these losses have derivatives available in closed form. The subset supplies the alternatives against which the model learns how its predictions affect the ordering of decisions.

Empirical comparisons find the resulting generic methods competitive with existing decision-focused approaches. The experiments also show that choosing the solution subset provides substantial control over runtime with limited impact on regret. This makes the ranking formulation useful both as an explanation of the learning goal and as a practical way to adjust computation while preserving decision quality in the evaluated settings.
icml-2022-decision-focused-learning-thro.tldr: Viewing decision-focused learning as ranking feasible solutions yields differentiable losses and practical runtime control with competitive empirical decision quality.

paragraphs: Clients in federated learning can differ in the attributes present in their local data. The paper argues that this attribute skew creates conflicting optimization directions when locally valid, non-causal attributes enter global aggregation. It also identifies a conflict between generalization and personalization when a single optimization stage handles these attributes together.

Disentangled federated learning separates domain-specific attributes and attributes that remain invariant across domains into two complementary branches. An alternating local-global optimization procedure trains the branches independently. This organization gives the model distinct places to handle local variation and shared information, directly addressing the mixing of attributes that the authors identify as a source of unstable learning.

The convergence analysis establishes that the system can converge stably even when incomplete client models take part in global aggregation. Experiments on both constructed and realistic attribute-skew datasets report higher performance, better interpretability, and faster convergence than the compared state-of-the-art federated methods. These results support separating the two kinds of attributes as a way to improve shared learning while retaining a role for client-specific information.
icml-2022-disentangled-federated-learnin.tldr: DFL separates shared and domain-specific attributes into independently trained branches, improving federated learning under attribute skew in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a feature-selection quantity called an e-value. Here, it measures how close the sampling distribution of parameter estimates for a model using fewer features is to the corresponding distribution for the full model. This makes the full model a reference for assessing which subsets retain the features needed to represent the relationship being learned.

Under general conditions, ordering models by their e-values separates those containing all essential features from those missing some. For p features, the proposed framework requires fitting only the full model and evaluating p+1 models. This substantially reduces the work relative to fitting and evaluating all 2^p possible subsets described in the paper’s comparison.

The implementation uses data depths and a fast resampling procedure, and the authors provide consistency results for feature selection. The framework applies to a broad range of parametric models. Experiments spanning several model settings and synthetic and real datasets suggest that it is a promising general alternative to methods designed for individual model classes, with its selection guarantees tied to the stated conditions.
icml-2022-feature-selection-using-e-valu.tldr: The proposed e-values compare parameter-estimate distributions to select essential features while requiring only one full-model fit and p+1 model evaluations.

paragraphs: This paper studies how the optimization formulation behind an explanation method affects the explanations it produces. Its starting point is Rate-Distortion Explanations, or RDE, which assigns relevance to input features for a neural network’s prediction. The authors reformulate RDE as a constrained optimization problem so that the sparsity of its relevance maps can be controlled precisely.

Sparsity concerns how many input features an explanation marks as relevant. Explicit control over it gives the method a direct handle on how selective an explanation should be. The reformulation also enables two extensions: a multi-rate version and a version that orders features by relevance. These provide additional ways to express which parts of an input matter for a prediction.

The authors investigate both deterministic and stochastic variants of the Frank-Wolfe algorithm for solving these explanation problems. In an established comparison test, both new RDE variants empirically outperform standard RDE and other baselines. The contribution links an optimization choice to concrete explanation capabilities and measured improvements in that evaluation, rather than presenting sparsity control as an end in itself.
icml-2022-interpretable-neural-networks-.tldr: A constrained RDE formulation gives precise sparsity control and enables explanation variants that outperform standard RDE and other baselines in the reported test.

paragraphs: Models can explain predictions by selecting relevant input features or by producing a natural-language account. These formats serve complementary purposes: selected features offer a compact view of supporting material, while text can give a fuller explanation. The paper addresses a gap in which models producing strong explanations often trail the best models on the underlying prediction task.

RExC is a self-rationalizing framework that grounds predictions and both explanation formats in background knowledge. It combines extractive rationales with natural-language explanations within the same framework. The authors report state-of-the-art task performance alongside explanations, as well as large improvements over previous state-of-the-art results in the quality of both explanation types.

The paper also uses perturbation analysis to examine how explanations relate to predictions. It finds a strong association between them, supplying evidence for a necessary property of faithful explanations. That result supports a connection between what the model says and what it predicts, but association alone does not establish complete faithfulness. The overall contribution combines predictive performance, complementary explanation formats, and evidence about their relationship.
icml-2022-knowledge-grounded-self-ration.tldr: RExC grounds predictions and two complementary explanation types in background knowledge, reporting strong task performance and improved explanation quality.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning must fit value functions that may change abruptly while also producing behavior that generalizes to new observations. This paper studies the tension between those goals through the learning dynamics of temporal-difference algorithms. It asks how the training process itself shapes what an agent learns, beyond whether it fits the value function.

The theoretical analysis shows that temporal-difference learning favors fitting non-smooth value components early in training and creates a second-order effect that discourages generalization. Experiments corroborate these findings across environments. On dense-reward tasks, networks trained with temporal-difference methods generalize less well between states than randomly initialized networks and networks trained using policy gradients.

The authors then investigate distilling the policy after training as a way to avoid this problem. They report improved generalization to new ProcGen environments and greater robustness to input perturbations. The results connect a particular learning dynamic to weaker generalization and identify post-training distillation as a useful response in the tested settings. They do not imply that fitting a value function and generalizing are always incompatible.
icml-2022-learning-dynamics-and-generali.tldr: Temporal-difference learning can discourage generalization, while post-training policy distillation improves transfer and input robustness in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Score-based generative models learn score functions and can use the resulting network to define a diffusion ordinary differential equation, or ODE, with exact likelihood evaluation. This paper examines whether the usual first-order score-matching objective is sufficient to maximize that ODE’s likelihood. The authors prove that it is not, identifying a gap between the two objectives.

They then show that the ODE’s negative likelihood can be bounded by controlling score-matching errors of the first, second, and third orders. This result motivates a higher-order denoising score-matching method for maximum-likelihood training. The algorithm also guarantees a bound on higher-order matching error in terms of training error and lower-order errors, connecting the new training procedure to the quantities needed by the analysis.

Experiments on synthetic data and CIFAR-10 show improved likelihood while retaining high generation quality. The contribution therefore distinguishes the ability to evaluate likelihood exactly from having a training objective that appropriately controls it. The theoretical bounds explain why higher-order matching is relevant, while the empirical results show that this change can improve likelihood without sacrificing the reported quality of generated samples.
icml-2022-maximum-likelihood-training-fo.tldr: Higher-order denoising score matching addresses a proven gap between first-order score matching and maximum-likelihood training of diffusion ODEs.

paragraphs: Self-interested learning agents can settle into outcomes that are bad for everyone. Opponent-shaping methods try to change this by influencing how other agents learn, but existing approaches can look ahead only a few updates, treat opponents as naive, and require access to their differentiable learning algorithms. Model-Free Opponent Shaping addresses these issues through a meta-game.

Each meta-step corresponds to an entire episode of the underlying game. The meta-state contains the players’ policies, and a meta-policy chooses a policy for the next episode. Generic model-free optimization then learns how these episode-level choices can shape opponents over longer horizons, avoiding the need to differentiate through an opponent’s learning procedure.

Empirically, M-FOS nearly optimally exploits both naive learners and more sophisticated methods. The authors report learning a zero-determinant extortion strategy in the iterated prisoner’s dilemma, which they describe as a first to their knowledge. In the same settings, meta-self-play produces socially optimal outcomes. They also demonstrate scaling to high-dimensional settings, showing that the framework can support both exploitation and mutually beneficial behavior depending on the interaction.
icml-2022-model-free-opponent-shaping-17.tldr: M-FOS learns episode-level policy updates that shape opponents over long horizons, producing strong exploitation and socially optimal meta-self-play in the evaluated settings.

paragraphs: A model that learns one physical system may struggle with another containing more elements, even when both obey the same laws. ModLaNet addresses this problem by organizing the model around reusable components. Its goal is to learn dynamics from simpler systems and extend that learning to more complex arrangements, such as pendulums with additional linked elements.

The framework models the energy of individual elements and combines them into a target system through Lagrangian mechanics. This physical structure gives the learned components a defined role in constructing the overall dynamics. Modularity also supports reusing trained networks and reducing network and dataset scale, making the organization of the model central to its generalization strategy.

The authors evaluate double-pendulum and three-body systems using small training datasets, reporting the best accuracy and data efficiency among the compared methods. They then reorganize trained models for multi-pendulum and multi-body systems to demonstrate reuse. These findings support transferring learned components across the tested system sizes, addressing a form of generalization that the relevant physics-informed networks discussed in the paper could not provide.
icml-2022-modlanets-learning-generalisab.tldr: ModLaNet combines reusable element-level energy models with Lagrangian mechanics to extend learned dynamics from simpler physical systems to more complex ones.

paragraphs: This paper improves sampling-based algorithms for CP and tensor ring decomposition. The starting point is alternating least squares, or ALS, methods whose work per iteration can be sublinear in the number of tensor entries when seeking a low-rank decomposition. That property makes the input’s sheer size less costly, but it does not resolve every source of computational growth.

Earlier methods still have a per-iteration cost that grows exponentially with the number of tensor modes when their parameters are chosen to obtain certain worst-case guarantees. The proposed sampling-based ALS methods remove that exponential dependence. This distinction matters because efficiency with respect to the number of entries can coexist with unfavorable scaling in the number of modes.

The authors provide a detailed theoretical analysis and apply their methods in a feature-extraction experiment. The main stated advance is the improved computational dependence while addressing the worst-case-guarantee setting. The experiment supplies an application of the methods, while the theoretical analysis supports the central claim about scaling. Together, they address an efficiency obstacle that remains even after sampling reduces dependence on total tensor size.
icml-2022-more-efficient-sampling-for-te.tldr: New sampling-based ALS methods remove exponential dependence on tensor modes in the cost of CP and tensor ring decomposition under worst-case-guarantee parameter choices.

paragraphs: Recommendation and advertising systems may need to assign several items at each step while respecting resource constraints and pursuing diversity or fairness. The paper studies this as an online matching problem formulated through constrained convex programming with high entropy. Existing approaches based on assigning a single item per iteration do not directly handle the multiple-slot setting.

Multiple slots make both gradient computation and resource allocation difficult because the needed closed-form solution is unavailable. The proposed OG-MA algorithm addresses these two obstacles separately. An efficient pooling procedure obtains a closed-form gradient, and a roulette-swapping procedure performs the allocation. Together, these components make the online update and assignment process computationally manageable.

The analysis establishes sublinear regret with linear cost per iteration. Sublinear regret means that the accumulated shortfall measured by regret grows more slowly than the number of rounds, so its average per round decreases. Experiments on synthetic and industrial datasets support the method’s speed and promise for multiple-slot matching. The contribution combines a theoretical performance guarantee with a practical allocation mechanism for the setting studied.
icml-2022-multi-slots-online-matching-wi.tldr: OG-MA handles multiple-slot online matching with efficient gradient computation and allocation, achieving sublinear regret and linear per-iteration cost.

paragraphs: Universal probabilistic programming languages can express models that challenge conventional inference algorithms. This paper focuses on nonparametric models and the need for a sampling state to move between different dimensions. It introduces NP-iMCMC as a framework for constructing Markov chain Monte Carlo inference algorithms for such models expressible in universal probabilistic programming languages.

The method builds on involutive MCMC and adds a general procedure for movement between dimensions. This allows numerous existing algorithms in that framework to be extended to nonparametric models. The authors prove the correctness of the resulting sampler, providing a mathematical foundation for these extensions rather than treating dimension changes as an informal modification to an existing method.

Empirical studies show that several algorithms retain their existing strengths after extension. The authors also apply the framework to Nonparametric HMC, which they identify as an instance of multiple-step NP-iMCMC, and construct several new nonparametric extensions with significant performance improvements. The contribution is therefore both a general construction method and evidence that useful sampling behavior can survive the move to variable-dimensional models.
icml-2022-nonparametric-involutive-marko.tldr: NP-iMCMC provides a proven framework for extending involutive MCMC algorithms to nonparametric models through movement between dimensions.

paragraphs: Nonlinear independent component analysis seeks to recover independent hidden components from observations formed by unknown nonlinear mixing. Identifiability asks whether those components can be determined, allowing certain ambiguities. Prior generalized contrastive learning results establish identifiability when the components are independent conditional on an auxiliary variable, but rely on unlimited data and ideal function learners.

This paper develops a finite-sample analysis to narrow that gap between theoretical recovery and practical learning. Its framework combines properties of the contrastive loss, statistical generalization analysis, and numerical differentiation. It also accounts for approximation error, recognizing that the chosen function learner may not perfectly express the relationship the analysis needs.

The resulting theory reveals a trade-off between learner complexity and expressiveness. Greater expressive capacity must be considered alongside what finite data can support, so idealized representational power alone does not settle the recovery question. Numerical experiments validate the theorems. The contribution makes identifiability analysis more relevant to limited-data learning while retaining the conditional-independence setting that motivates the contrastive formulation.
icml-2022-on-finite-sample-identifiabili.tldr: A finite-sample analysis of contrastive nonlinear ICA accounts for approximation error and exposes a trade-off between learner complexity and expressiveness.

paragraphs: Federated learning often assumes that useful labels are readily available. Removing that assumption requires unsupervised methods that also cope with differences in clients’ data and systems, large participant counts, and communication constraints. Orchestra addresses this combination of requirements through a clustering procedure designed around the hierarchy of the federation.

The method coordinates distributed clustering so that clients’ data are partitioned into distinguishable groups in a globally consistent way. This gives local learning a shared organization across participants. The approach is motivated by the limitations of directly adapting centralized self-supervised methods, which were not designed around the operating conditions and coordination needs of federated training.

The authors show that Orchestra’s pipeline guarantees good generalization under a linear probe, which assesses learned representations using a linear predictor. They also report better performance than alternative techniques across variations in heterogeneity, client count, participation ratio, and local training epochs. The findings connect a consistent clustering structure to useful learned representations and show its value across the tested federated conditions, rather than relying on labels to coordinate learning.
icml-2022-orchestra-unsupervised-federat.tldr: Orchestra coordinates globally consistent clustering across clients to support unsupervised federated learning and strong linear-probe generalization.

paragraphs: Dynamic mechanism design studies repeated interactions between a seller and agents whose rewards may depend on time and state. This paper considers interactions modeled as a Markov decision process when neither rewards nor transition rules are known beforehand. The aim is to learn a mechanism from an already collected dataset, making the problem an offline learning task.

The authors use offline reinforcement learning with function approximation to address large state spaces. Their algorithm follows a pessimism principle and assumes mild conditions on both the expressiveness of the function class and the coverage provided by the dataset. It does not require uniform data coverage, a distinction the authors identify as a first for offline reinforcement learning in dynamic mechanism design, to their knowledge.

The learned mechanisms approximately satisfy efficiency, individual rationality, and truthfulness. These concern desirable collective outcomes, agents’ willingness to participate, and incentives to report honestly. The qualification matters: the result provides approximate properties under the stated learning assumptions. It connects learning from incomplete prior experience to mechanism design while explicitly accounting for the uncertainty associated with offline data.
icml-2022-pessimism-meets-vcg-learning-d.tldr: A pessimistic offline RL method learns dynamic mechanisms with approximate efficiency, individual rationality, and truthfulness without requiring uniform data coverage.

paragraphs: This paper explains deep networks by measuring how information about individual inputs is discarded as computation moves through successive layers. Its focus is the information a layer retains about particular input variables. That provides a perspective on internal processing that can reveal how the treatment of input information changes throughout a network.

The authors define two entropy-based measures. One captures the discarding of pixel-level information used during forward propagation; the other captures uncertainty about reconstructing the input. These offer complementary views of the input information contained in a layer. The proposed metrics also support fair comparisons across layers and across different networks, making comparisons central to their explanatory value.

Using these measures, the paper studies information-processing efficiency and reports strong connections with network performance. Experiments demonstrate their usefulness for analyzing established networks and explaining existing deep-learning techniques. The analysis operates at the level of individual pixels, distinguishing it from information-bottleneck analysis of features relative to a sample distribution. Its contribution is a comparable, input-specific account of information loss, with evidence connecting that account to network behavior.
icml-2022-quantification-and-analysis-of.tldr: Two entropy-based metrics track pixel-level information loss through networks and support fair comparisons across layers and architectures.

paragraphs: Allocating resources across several submodular objectives raises a robustness question: how can an allocation perform reliably across the objectives being considered? This paper approaches that question through quantile maximization. A quantile-based objective makes a selected position in the distribution of outcomes part of the optimization target, giving robustness an explicit mathematical formulation.

The authors first show that finding an exact solution is computationally intractable. They then introduce a softmax-based proxy for the quantile function and show that it is suited to submodular optimization. This relaxation leads to SOFTSAT, a simple algorithm accompanied by theoretical properties and new approximation guarantees. The proxy is the bridge from the difficult exact problem to a tractable algorithmic approach.

Numerical experiments compare SOFTSAT with state-of-the-art methods across a collection of real-world applications. The reported results support its efficiency and robustness, particularly in online scenarios. The paper thus combines a formal treatment of the computational difficulty with an approximate solution and practical evidence. Its guarantees concern the proposed approximation approach, while the online suitability is supported by the numerical evaluations.
icml-2022-robustness-in-multi-objective-.tldr: SOFTSAT uses a softmax proxy for quantile maximization to obtain robust submodular allocations with approximation guarantees and promising online performance.

paragraphs: Automatic music transcription converts a recording into musical content, but collecting training labels for many instruments is difficult. Digitized scores can help, yet aligning them to performances has often required substantial human effort. Note_EM addresses this bottleneck by learning a transcriber and aligning each score to its corresponding recording in one fully automated process.

The training approach combines unaligned supervision with pseudo-labels and pitch-shift augmentation. This makes recordings collected outside controlled settings usable for training while expanding the instrumental variety the system can handle. The central contribution is the joint treatment of alignment and transcription learning, allowing the score-performance pairs to provide supervision without manually establishing their timing alignment first.

Using synthetic data and unaligned supervision, the authors report state-of-the-art note-level accuracy on MAPS and large improvements in cross-dataset evaluations. They also obtain comparable results when training on a small, readily collected dataset and propose more accurate alternative labels for MusicNet. These findings support both transcription performance and the practical value of reducing the effort needed to assemble usable training material.
icml-2022-unaligned-supervision-for-auto.tldr: Note_EM jointly aligns scores and trains a music transcriber, enabling strong multi-instrument transcription from recordings with unaligned supervision.

paragraphs: SMODICE is an offline imitation-learning algorithm that does not require expert actions. It is derived by matching state occupancy, meaning the pattern of states associated with the behavior or examples being imitated. This focus allows the method to use information about desirable states even when the expert’s action choices are unavailable.

The authors derive a regression-based objective and use Fenchel duality to obtain a simple optimization procedure. For tabular Markov decision processes, they also provide an analytic solution. The same framework covers imitation from observations, imitation when the expert has different dynamics or morphology, and example-based reinforcement learning. The paper shows that the last of these can also be expressed as state-occupancy matching.

Evaluations span gridworlds and high-dimensional offline benchmarks. The reported results show effectiveness across all three settings and significant improvements over prior state-of-the-art methods. The main value is the unification: one state-based learning formulation handles several forms of supervision that do not supply matching expert actions. The empirical evidence supports that versatility across the environments and problem settings evaluated.
icml-2022-versatile-offline-imitation-fr.tldr: SMODICE uses state-occupancy matching to learn offline from observations or examples without expert actions, including settings with mismatched expert dynamics or morphology.

paragraphs: Designing reinforcement-learning rewards can require access to a system’s true state, while collecting demonstrations or goal images can be labor-intensive. This paper investigates describing the desired task in ordinary text instead. Its framework uses large vision-language models such as CLIP to generate a reward signal from a goal description and raw image observations.

The generated reward is then used to train a policy for the task. This directly addresses the reward-specification stage: the task description and observed pixels provide the inputs for reward generation. The approach differs from earlier text-conditioned policy work discussed in the paper, where rewards still depended on true-state information or labeled expert demonstrations.

The authors evaluate the framework on control and robotic manipulation tasks. They then distill separately learned task policies into one policy conditioned on goal text. This combined policy can generalize without additional task-specific training to new tasks involving unseen objects and unseen goal descriptions. The work therefore connects language-based reward construction with a shared policy that supports the reported zero-shot generalization.
icml-2022-zero-shot-reward-specification.tldr: Vision-language models turn goal text and pixels into rewards, enabling policies that can be distilled into a text-conditioned policy with zero-shot task generalization.
